rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the scouting gradient fixed and raise temperature to probe selectivity changes in the crowded central cluster and nearly coeluting last pair. All peaks currently elute comfortably before 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent gradient shallowing.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to establish whether cooling offers better selectivity than heating. This separates temperature effects from slope effects before refining the gradient around the most promising region.

Cooling gives the strongest selectivity so far, with only two pairs below target. Shallower elution at 25 C should increase their separation while the current 6.37-minute last peak leaves room before the time penalty begins.

The central critical pair appears to approach or cross coelution as the gradient becomes shallower, while the late pair improves. Test a still shallower slope beyond that region, using a higher starting organic fraction to keep the last peak near the unpenalized window.

Further reduce the gradient slope at the promising 25 C condition to increase separation beyond the central pair's apparent order crossing. Keeping the same starting fraction isolates the slope response; the late pair already exceeds the resolution target.

All pairs are now fully resolved, so shorten the gradient to remove the small time penalty. A 24-minute gradient should place the last peak below 10 minutes while retaining adequate separation of the central critical pair.
The maximum CRF is established at injection 7. Shorten the gradient one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method, with the central pair's resolution of 1.93 providing a modest margin.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing the gradient slope. That shallower slope may protect the central pair, which is only just resolved in injection 8.

Test a modest temperature increase at the faster starting composition to shift selectivity in the central critical pair. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this trial explores whether temperature can recover resolution at shorter retention.

Apply modest heating to the fastest confirmed fully resolved gradient to reduce retention time. Monitor both the central cluster and the last pair, since temperature can improve speed while bringing previously separated peaks together.

At 30 C, the two starting compositions bracket a tradeoff between neighboring central pairs. A shallower gradient from 0.25 may raise the deficient pair above 1.5 while preserving the adjacent pair's margin and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

The 30 C trials show competing resolution limits, so explore a faster selectivity region at 25 C. A higher starting fraction and steeper gradient may separate the central pair on the opposite side of its crossing; the late pair will be the other key constraint.

Steepen the gradient to move the central pair farther from its apparent crossing on this faster branch. The late pair has some resolution margin at 1.85, so this tests whether full resolution can be achieved around five minutes.

Increase the slope modestly from 0.0542 to 0.060 organic fraction per minute to improve the central pair without sacrificing too much late-pair resolution. This targets the narrow fully resolved region suggested by the last two runs.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step to shorten the fastest fully resolved method. The slightly shallower slope may preserve the marginal late pair, while the higher starting fraction may improve central-pair selectivity on this branch.

Reduce the slope slightly to recover the newly limiting central pair while retaining the shorter elution window. The other pairs have resolution margin, and the late pair should also benefit from the shallower gradient.

Test a higher starting fraction with a compensating shallower slope to seek an even faster fully resolved method. The reduced slope is intended to protect the central pair that became limiting when the starting fraction was raised previously.

Keep injection 17 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method and probe a higher-temperature selectivity region with its gradient. This tests whether an elution-order change can enable further shortening rather than continuing the unfavorable starting-fraction trend.

Return to 25 C and halve the slope at the higher starting fraction to test whether the central limiting pair can recover full resolution. The previous run at this starting fraction eluted all peaks by four minutes, leaving ample room for a shallower gradient without a time penalty.

Injection 17 remains the fastest fully resolved method. Test whether increasing the starting fraction moves the limiting central pair through its selectivity crossing into a faster resolved region, while monitoring compression of the earliest peaks.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 17's starting composition and slope. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after its observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should retain full resolution with a lower final organic fraction.

Test one temperature step above the compact, fully resolved method to seek a shorter elution time. This small change may preserve selectivity better than the unsuccessful 50 C trial; injection 22 remains the fallback.

Return to 25 C and shorten the programmed gradient to its minimum while preserving the successful initial slope. The hold begins after the central cluster has eluted, so this tests whether a lower final organic fraction retains full resolution and an unpenalized last-peak time.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower gradient around the fastest fully resolved condition, seeking greater resolution margin while remaining well below 10 minutes. Injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed compact method with maximum CRF.
